contests.title: Allow judges to deny bail in more cases
contests.label: Public Question #1: Ratification of State Constitutional Amendment (Article 1, Section 17)

ballotText.t: Currently, under the Constitution of the State of Indiana, a person charged with murder or treason is not entitled to be released on bail if the proof is evident or the presumption strong. Shall the Constitution of the State of Indiana be amended to provide that a person charged with an offense other than murder or treason is not entitled to bail if: (1) the proof is evident or the presumption strong; and (2) the state proves by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions will reasonably protect the safety of any other person or the community. (This question concerns Article 1, Section 17 of the Constitution of the State of Indiana.)

summary.t: Today Indiana's constitution lets judges hold someone without bail only for murder or treason. A Yes vote lets judges also deny bail for any other charge when the proof is strong and prosecutors show by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions would keep others safe.

contests.yes: Judges can hold people charged with any offense without bail if the court finds no release conditions would keep others safe.
contests.no: Bail stays guaranteed for every charge except murder and treason.

pro.t: Supporters, led by sponsor Rep. Chris Jeter, say judges are now forced to release people who pose clear risks, including people who commit violent crimes while out on bail.

con.t: Critics say it lets people sit in jail for months without a conviction and could fall hardest on marginalized communities.

supporters.t: Passed the Senate 43-2 and the House 75-11. Every Republican voted yes; Democrats split.

tags.why: Yes widens pretrial detention, a tougher-enforcement step.

quality.t: The amendment covers every offense, not a list of violent crimes as some states use. Lawmakers rejected a change that would have excluded misdemeanors and Level 6 felonies, and Sen. Rodney Pol questioned whether the ballot wording shows how broadly it could apply.

contests.title: Let city and town court judges live in a neighboring county
contests.label: Public Question #2: Ratification of State Constitutional Amendment (Article 6, Section 6)

ballotText.t: Shall the Constitution of the State of Indiana be amended to permit the judge of a city or town court to reside in: (1) the county in which the court is located; or (2) the bordering county closest to the city or town in which the court is located? (This question concerns Article 6, Section 6 of the Constitution of the State of Indiana.)

summary.t: City and town court judges would be allowed to live anywhere in the court's county, or in the bordering county closest to the city or town, instead of meeting the current residency rule.

contests.yes: City and town court judges may live in the court's county or the closest bordering county.
contests.no: The current residency rule for city and town court judges stays.

pro.t: Widens the pool of lawyers who can serve on small city and town courts.

con.t: Judges could live outside the community and county they serve.

supporters.t: Passed by the General Assembly as HB 1019; the House vote was 66-25.
